slides.title: Introduction to Threads
slides.body: Introduction to Threads
slides.notes: First of all We'll be learning about the Introduction To Threads.

slides.title: Process Control Block
slides.body:
Process Execution State
Program Counter determines the next instruction to be executed
Results in a stream of instructions which are often referred to as a thread of execution
slides.notes: Now, among the information stored in the PCB, the Program Counter plays an important role. It keeps track of the next instruction to be executed, ensuring the process resumes from the correct point. This continuous sequence of instruction execution is referred to as a thread of execution.

slides.title: Introduction to Threads
slides.body:
What is a Thread?
A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process
slides.notes: Now, let's move on to the concept of threads. While a process represents a running program, a thread is the smallest unit that actually performs the execution within that process. A single process can have one or more threads working inside it.

slides.title: Introduction to Threads
slides.body:
What Does a Thread Contain?
Each thread has
A program counter
A register set
A stack space
Address Space
Execution State
Data
Files
Code
Registers
Stack
Thread
slides.notes: Next, a thread shares the process resources such as the code, data, address space, and open files. At the same time, each thread maintains its own program counter, register set, execution state, and stack, allowing it to execute independently within the same process.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body:
Advantages of Threads
Threads are lightweight
Less time to create and terminate
Faster to context switch between threads
Quicker communication between threads

slides.notes: Moving on, threads are considered lightweight because they share the same process resources instead of creating separate ones. As a result, creating and terminating threads takes less time, context switching is faster, and communication between threads is more efficient.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body: Multithreading
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Multithreading

slides.title: Introduction to Multithreading
slides.body:
What is Multithreading?
Multithreading is the ability of a process to create and run multiple threads at the same time, allowing different parts of the program to execute concurrently
slides.notes: Now, instead of relying on a single thread, a process can create multiple threads to perform different tasks concurrently. This approach, known as multithreading, helps improve responsiveness and makes better use of the CPU by allowing multiple parts of the same application to execute simultaneously.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body:
Characteristics of Multithreading
A process can have multiple threads
Threads share the same code, data, and files of the process
Each thread has its own registers and stack
Threads can run on different CPU cores - improving performance
slides.notes: Next, a single process can create multiple threads that work together by sharing the same code, data, and files. At the same time, each thread maintains its own registers and stack, allowing them to execute independently. On multi-core systems, these threads can also run on different CPU cores, improving overall performance.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body:
Benefits
Responsiveness
Resource Sharing
Economy
Scalability
slides.notes: Moving on, multithreading offers several advantages that improve the performance and efficiency of an application. The key benefits include responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, and scalability. Let's understand each of these in detail.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body:
Single vs Multi-Threaded Process
Single-Threaded Process
slides.notes: Next, this diagram illustrates the difference between a single-threaded and a multi-threaded process. A single-threaded process relies on one thread to perform all tasks, whereas a multi-threaded process contains multiple threads. These threads share the process resources, such as Code, data and files, but each thread maintains its own registers, program counter, and stack, allowing them to execute independently.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body:
Single vs Multi-Threaded Process
Only one thread of execution
Example: Basic command-line calculator program
Single-Threaded Process
Multi-Threaded Process
Contains two or more threads running concurrently
Example: web browser (parallel threads manage rendering & video)
A process can run with one thread or multiple threads depending on how tasks need to be executed
slides.notes: Next, a process may operate with either a single thread or multiple threads, depending on the nature of the application. For example, a basic command-line calculator uses a single thread since it performs one task at a time. In contrast, a web browser uses multiple threads to handle activities like page rendering and video playback simultaneously, providing a smoother user experience.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body: Key Differences

slides.title: Single-Threaded Process
slides.body:
Advantages
Advantages
Simple to design and manage
Easy to test and debug
Uses fewer system resources
Good for small, sequential programs
slides.notes: Moving on, single-threaded processes are suitable for applications with straightforward execution. They are simpler to design, easier to test and debug, consume fewer system resources, and work well for programs that execute tasks in a sequential manner.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body:
Advantages of Multi-Threaded Process
Advantages
Better performance for multitasking
Efficient CPU utilization
Allows parallel execution on multi-core processors
Faster execution of independent tasks
Good for real-time applications (e.g., chat apps, games)
slides.notes:
Moving on, multi-threaded processes can handle multiple activities more efficiently, leading to better multitasking and improved CPU utilization. They also support parallel execution on multi-core processors, complete independent tasks faster,
 and are well suited for real-time applications such as chat applications and games.

slides.title: Multithreading
slides.body: When to Use What?
slides.notes: Finally, the choice between a single-threaded and a multi-threaded approach depends on the application's requirements. If the tasks are simple and sequential, a single thread is usually sufficient. However, if responsiveness, parallel execution, and efficient utilization of CPU cores are important, a multi-threaded approach is the better choice.

slides.title: Thread Types and Models
slides.body: Thread Types and Models
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Thread Types and Models

slides.title: Thread Types
slides.body:
Types of Threads
Kernel-Level Threads (KLTs)
User-Level Threads (ULTs)
Threads can be implemented at two different levels:
slides.notes: Now, threads can be categorized based on where they are managed. The two main types are User-Level Threads, which are managed in user space, and Kernel-Level Threads, which are managed directly by the operating system. Let's understand each of them in detail.

slides.title: Types of Threads
slides.body:
User-Level Threads (ULTs)
Threads managed entirely in user space by a thread library
The operating system does not know these threads exist
User Level Threads
slides.notes: Next, let's begin with User-Level Threads. These threads are created and managed entirely in user space using a thread library. Since the operating system is unaware of their existence, all thread management is handled without direct involvement of the kernel.

slides.title: User-Level Threads (ULTs)
slides.body:
How ULTs Work?
User Level THreads
Thread library handles creation, scheduling, and switching
Kernel sees only a single process
All operations happen in user space
slides.notes: Moving on, in this approach, the thread library is responsible for creating, scheduling, and switching between threads. Since all these operations take place in user space, the kernel treats them as a single process rather than multiple threads.

slides.title: User-Level Threads (ULTs)
slides.body:
Advantages of User-Level Threads
Advantages
Fast: No kernel involvement for creation/switching
Portable: Works on any OS
Flexible: Custom scheduling possible
slides.notes: Next, because the kernel is not involved in managing these threads, operations such as thread creation and switching are much faster. They are also portable across different operating systems, and the thread library provides the flexibility to implement custom scheduling policies.

slides.title: User-Level Threads (ULTs)
slides.body:
Disadvantages of User-Level Threads
Disadvantages
Blocking: One thread blocking halts the entire process
No true parallelism: Cannot use multiple CPU cores
Complex: Requires careful programming
slides.notes: Moving on, User-Level Threads also have some limitations. If one thread becomes blocked, the entire process is affected. Since the kernel treats all threads as a single process, they cannot execute in parallel on multiple CPU cores. In addition, managing these threads correctly requires careful programming.

slides.title: Types of Threads
slides.body:
Kernel-Level Threads (KLTs)
Threads that are managed directly by the operating system kernel
The kernel is fully aware of each thread and schedules them individually
slides.notes: Next, unlike User-Level Threads, Kernel-Level Threads are created and managed directly by the operating system kernel. Since the kernel is aware of every thread, it can schedule each one independently, enabling more efficient execution.

slides.title: Kernel-Level Threads (KLTs)
slides.body:
How KLTs Work?
Kernel is aware of all threads
Kernel schedules threads, not processes
Each thread can be scheduled on different CPU core
slides.notes: Moving on, in Kernel-Level Threads, the operating system manages every thread individually. The kernel is aware of all the threads, schedules them independently, and can even assign different threads to different CPU cores for better performance.

slides.title: Kernel-Level Threads (KLTs)
slides.body:
Advantages of Kernel-Level Threads
Advantages
True Parallelism: Kernel can schedule threads on different CPU cores simultaneously
No Blocking Issues: If one thread blocks, kernel schedules another thread from the same process
Better I/O Handling: Blocking system calls don't affect other threads
slides.notes: Next, Kernel-Level Threads offer several advantages. They support true parallel execution by allowing different threads to run on separate CPU cores. If one thread is waiting for an I/O operation, the kernel can continue executing other threads from the same process, resulting in better CPU utilization and improved I/O performance.

slides.title: Kernel-Level Threads (KLTs)
slides.body:
Disadvantages of Kernel-Level Threads
Disadvantages
Slower: Thread operations require system calls (kernel mode switching)
Overhead: Kernel must maintain information for every thread
slides.notes: Finally, Kernel-Level Threads also come with some trade-offs. Since thread operations involve the kernel, actions like creating or switching threads take more time. Additionally, the kernel has to maintain information for every thread, which increases system overhead.

slides.title: Thread Operations & Multicore
slides.body: Thread Operations & Multicore
slides.notes: Next , we will be learning about the Thread Operations & Multicore.

slides.title: Thread Models
slides.body:
Multi-Threading Models
How User and Kernel Threads Relate?
Operating systems can map user-level threads to kernel-level threads in different ways, this is called the multi-threading model
Many-to-Many Model
Many-to-One Model
One-to-One Model
Multi-threading model
slides.notes: Now, we've seen how User-Level Threads and Kernel-Level Threads work individually. The next question is how these two are connected. The operating system establishes this relationship using different multithreading models, namely Many-to-One, One-to-One, and Many-to-Many. Let's explore each model one by one.

slides.title: Multi-Threading Models
slides.body:
Many-to-Many Model
Multiple user threads mapped to multiple kernel threads
Independent execution: blocking of one thread does not affect others
High concurrency and efficient parallelism
User Threads
Kernel Threads
slides.notes: Next, in the Many-to-Many model, multiple user threads are mapped to multiple kernel threads. This allows several threads to execute independently, so if one thread becomes blocked, the others can continue running. As a result, this model provides better concurrency and efficient parallel execution.

slides.title: Multi-Threading Models
slides.body:
Many-to-one Model
Multiple user threads mapped to a single kernel thread
Blocking in any thread halts the entire process
Lightweight but limited in multiprocessor environments
User Threads
Kernel Threads
slides.notes: Next, in the Many-to-One model, multiple user threads are associated with a single kernel thread. Because they all depend on the same kernel thread, if one thread gets blocked, the entire process has to wait. Although this model is lightweight, it cannot take full advantage of multiple CPU cores.

slides.title: Multi-Threading Models
slides.body:
One-to-One Models
Each user thread mapped to a separate kernel thread
Supports true parallel execution on multiple CPU cores
Each thread consumes more system resources
User Threads
Kernel Threads
slides.notes: Finally, in the One-to-One model, every user thread is paired with its own kernel thread. This allows threads to execute in parallel on multiple CPU cores. However, since each thread requires a separate kernel thread, this model consumes more system resources.

slides.title: Thread Models
slides.body: Multithreading Execution Types
slides.notes: Now, apart from the thread mapping models, threads can also be categorized based on how they are scheduled and how they execute tasks. Based on scheduling, we have Cooperative and Preemptive execution, while task execution can be Synchronous or Asynchronous. Let's understand each of these execution types in detail.

slides.title: Multithreading Execution Types
slides.body:
Cooperative Multithreading
The processor runs one thread at a time, and switches to another thread only at specific points decided by the program
A thread runs completely until it reaches a “yield” or waiting point
Only then the CPU gives control to another thread
Threads cooperate and must give up control voluntarily
slides.notes: Next, let's begin with Cooperative Multithreading. In this approach, a thread continues executing until it voluntarily gives up the CPU, either by reaching a yield point or waiting for an operation to complete. Only then does another thread get a chance to execute, so the threads must cooperate with one another.

slides.title: Cooperative Multithreading
slides.body:
Characteristics
If one thread misbehaves (never yields), other threads get blocked
Low overhead
Simple to implement
slides.notes:
Moving on, Cooperative Multithreading is relatively simple to implement and has low overhead, because threads voluntarily yield control of the CPU.
Here, yield control means a running thread voluntarily gives up the CPU so another thread can execute, usually at a yield point or when waiting for an operation.
However, if a thread does not yield control, it can block other threads from running, affecting application responsiveness.

slides.title: Cooperative Multithreading
slides.body:
Example
Simple embedded systems
Old single-core systems
Early operating systems
slides.notes: Next, Cooperative Multithreading was commonly used in early operating systems, old single-core computers, and simple embedded systems, where applications were relatively simple and threads could reliably cooperate by yielding control when required.

slides.title: Multithreading Execution Types
slides.body:
Preemptive Multithreading
The processor switches between threads automatically, based on a timer or scheduler
CPU interrupts a running thread at fixed intervals
Scheduler picks another thread
Threads don’t need to yield voluntarily
Ensures fair CPU sharing
slides.notes:
Next, in Preemptive Multithreading, 
the operating system automatically decides when a thread should stop executing. At regular intervals, the scheduler interrupts the currently running thread and assigns the CPU to another one. This ensures that all threads get a fair share of CPU time without having to yield control themselves.

slides.title: Preemptive Multithreading
slides.body:
Characteristics
Slightly higher overhead due to frequent switching
True multitasking
Better responsiveness
slides.notes: Moving on, Preemptive Multithreading provides better responsiveness because the operating system can switch between threads whenever required. This enables true multitasking, although the frequent thread switching introduces a small amount of additional overhead.

slides.title: Preemptive Multithreading
slides.body:
Example
Modern OS (Windows, Linux, macOS)
Multi-core processors
slides.notes: Next, Preemptive Multithreading is the standard approach used in modern operating systems such as Windows, Linux, and macOS. It is also well suited for multi-core processors, where multiple threads can be scheduled efficiently across different CPU cores.

slides.title: Overview
slides.body:
Thread Operations
Thread Operations
slides.notes: Now, let's move on to the common operations performed on threads. We'll understand how threads are created, terminated, cancelled, and synchronized, along with the role each of these operations plays in multithreaded applications.

slides.title: Thread Operations
slides.body:
Thread Creation & Termination
Thread Creation
Thread Termination
A thread finishes execution normally after completing its task
Can also terminate itself using explicit functions 
Example: pthread_exit())
A new thread is created to execute a specific task
Requires specifying the function/task the thread will run
Example: pthread_create() in C/C++
slides.notes: Next, every thread goes through a lifecycle that begins with its creation and ends with its termination. During creation, the task or function that the thread should execute is specified, using functions such as pthread_create(). After completing its assigned work, the thread exits automatically or can terminate itself explicitly using pthread_exit().

slides.title: Thread Operations
slides.body:
Thread Cancellation Mechanism
Thread Cancellation
Terminating a thread before it completes naturally
Thread Cancellation Types
Used for stopping long-running tasks or exiting threads waiting indefinitely
Asynchronous
Deferred
Immediate termination
Terminates at safe cancellation points
slides.notes: Moving on, sometimes a thread needs to be stopped before it finishes its task. This is known as thread cancellation. It can happen asynchronously, where the thread is terminated immediately, or deferred, where it exits only at safe cancellation points. This mechanism is commonly used to stop long-running tasks or threads waiting indefinitely.

slides.title: Thread Operations
slides.body:
Thread Synchronization Mechanism
Thread Synchronization
Ensures multiple threads access shared resources safely
Thread Synchronization Mechanisms
slides.notes:
Finally, when multiple threads work with the same data or resources, they must be coordinated to avoid conflicts. This is achieved through thread synchronization, using mechanisms such as mutexes or locks, semaphores, 
and condition variables to ensure safe and controlled access to shared resources.

slides.title: What is Multicore Programming?
slides.body:
Task 
Definition
Multicore programming is the practice of writing software that can execute tasks concurrently on multiple CPU cores to improve performance and efficiency
Software
Task Executing concurrently
slides.notes: Now, let's move on to Multicore Programming. Instead of executing tasks one after another, applications are designed to run multiple tasks concurrently across different CPU cores. This improves overall performance and makes more efficient use of the available processing power.

slides.title: Multicore Programming
slides.body:
Key Points
Modern CPUs have multiple cores, allowing true parallel execution
Multicore programming leverages threads or processes to run tasks simultaneously
It is essential for high-performance computing, real-time systems, and responsive applications
slides.notes: Next, modern computers are equipped with multiple CPU cores, making it possible to execute tasks in parallel. By using threads or processes, applications can distribute work across these cores, resulting in better performance, improved responsiveness, and efficient execution in areas such as high-performance computing and real-time systems.

slides.title: Multicore Programming
slides.body:
Examples
A web server handling multiple client requests on different cores
A video processing application dividing frames across multiple cores
slides.notes: Finally, multicore programming is widely used in real-world applications. For example, a web server can handle multiple client requests simultaneously by distributing them across different CPU cores. Similarly, a video processing application can process different video frames in parallel, significantly reducing the overall processing time.

slides.title: Multicore Programming
slides.body:
Challenges 
Breaking a program into independent tasks that can run in parallel
Task Decomposition
Ensuring all cores have roughly equal work to avoid idle cores
Load Balancing
slides.notes: Next, developing applications for multicore systems comes with a few challenges. The work must first be divided into independent tasks that can run in parallel. At the same time, the workload should be distributed evenly across all CPU cores to ensure that no core remains idle while others are overloaded.

slides.title: Multicore Programming
slides.body:
Avoid race conditions and ensure correct results when threads share data
Synchronization & Data Sharing
Not all tasks benefit from additional cores, some programs have sequential bottlenecks
Scalability
Challenges
slides.notes: Moving on, another challenge is ensuring that multiple threads access shared data safely without causing incorrect results or race conditions. In addition, applications should be able to scale efficiently as more CPU cores are added, although some programs are limited by tasks that must still execute sequentially.

slides.title: Multicore Programming
slides.body:
Concurrent execution makes bugs non-deterministic and harder to reproduce
 Debugging & Testing
Threads may compete for memory, cache, or I/O resources, reducing efficiency
Resource Contention
Challenges
slides.notes: Another challenge in multicore programming is debugging and testing. Since multiple threads execute concurrently, bugs can become non-deterministic and difficult to reproduce. Resource contention is another challenge, where threads compete for shared resources like memory, cache, or I/O devices, reducing overall system efficiency.

slides.title: Concurrency & Parallelism
slides.body: Concurrency & Parallelism
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Concurrency & Parallelism

slides.title: Difference
slides.body:
Multiple tasks make progress at the same time (logically)
Tasks may interleave on a single core
Example: Multithreading on a single CPU
Concurrency
Parallelism vs Concurrency
Multiple tasks run literally at the same time on multiple cores
Requires multi-core hardware
Example: Running 4 threads on 4 CPU cores
Parallelism
slides.notes: Finally, although concurrency and parallelism are often used interchangeably, they are different. In concurrency, multiple tasks make progress by taking turns, even on a single CPU core. In parallelism, multiple tasks execute at the same time on different CPU cores. For example, multithreading on a single-core processor demonstrates concurrency, while running four threads simultaneously on four CPU cores is an example of parallelism.

slides.title: Types of Parallelism
slides.body:
Data Parallelism
 Task Parallelism
Bit-level Parallelism
Pipeline Parallelism
 Instruction-level Parallelism (ILP)
Overview
slides.notes: Now, let's explore the different types of parallelism used in computer systems. Depending on what is executed in parallel, parallelism can be classified into Bit-level Parallelism, Instruction-level Parallelism, Pipeline Parallelism, Data Parallelism, and Task Parallelism. We'll understand each of these types one by one.

slides.title: Types of Parallelism
slides.body:
Data Parallelism
Same operation on different chunks of data
Example: Processing different parts of an array in parallel
Operation A
slides.notes:
Next, Data Parallelism focuses on performing the same operation on different parts of data simultaneously.
For example, when processing a large array, the array can be divided into smaller chunks, and each chunk can be processed in parallel. This helps reduce the overall execution time significantly.

slides.title: Types of Parallelism
slides.body:
Task Parallelism
Different tasks run in parallel
Each task performs a different operation
Example: One thread reads input; another processes data
Operation A
Operation B
slides.notes: Next, Task Parallelism involves executing different tasks at the same time. Instead of performing the same operation on different data, each task carries out a separate function. For example, one thread can read the input while another thread processes the data concurrently.

slides.title: Types of Parallelism
slides.body:
Bit-level Parallelism
Increases processor word size to process more bits at once
slides.notes: Moving on, Bit-level Parallelism improves performance by increasing the processor's word size, allowing it to process more bits in a single operation. This enables the CPU to handle larger amounts of data more efficiently.

slides.title: Types of Parallelism
slides.body:
Instruction-level Parallelism (ILP)
CPU executes multiple instructions simultaneously
Example: pipelining in processors
slides.notes: Next, Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP) allows the CPU to execute multiple instructions simultaneously, improving overall performance. A common example is instruction pipelining, where different stages of multiple instructions are processed concurrently.

slides.title: Types of Parallelism
slides.body:
Pipeline Parallelism
Example: Assembly line model
Tasks broken into stages
Each stage runs in parallel on different data
slides.notes: Finally, Pipeline Parallelism divides a task into multiple stages, with each stage working on different data simultaneously. This is similar to an assembly line, where different stages operate in parallel to improve the overall throughput and efficiency.
